Title: How to Test Open Source Contributions Locally
Desc: Learn how to safely test open source contributions on your own machine before submitting a pull request. Discover practical workflows that help you catch issues early and improve your chances of getting merged.
Author: M Ramzan Ch
Data:
## One of the fastest ways to get an open source pull request rejected is simple:

```text
Submit Code
↓
Never Test It
```

Maintainers expect contributors to verify their changes before opening a pull request.

Testing locally helps you:

* Catch bugs early
* Avoid breaking existing features
* Reduce review time
* Improve contribution quality

Fortunately, the process is easier than many beginners think.

---

## Why Local Testing Matters

Imagine this workflow:

```text id="bad-workflow"
Write Code
↓
Submit PR
↓
CI Fails
↓
Fix Problems
↓
Repeat
```

Now compare:

```text id="good-workflow"
Write Code
↓
Test Locally
↓
Fix Issues
↓
Submit PR
```

The second workflow saves everyone time.

---

## Step 1: Fork the Repository

Most open source contributions start with a fork.

Workflow:

```text id="fork-flow"
Original Repository
↓
Fork
↓
Your GitHub Account
```

This gives you your own copy of the project.

---

## Step 2: Clone the Repository

After forking:

```bash id="clone-repo"
git clone https://github.com/your-username/project-name.git
```

Move into the project folder:

```bash id="enter-folder"
cd project-name
```

Now the project exists on your machine.

---

![Open source repository cloned into a local development environment](https://images.unsplash.com/photo-1555066931-4365d14bab8c)

## Step 3: Read the Documentation

Before running anything:

Look for:

```text id="docs"
README.md
CONTRIBUTING.md
```

These files often explain:

* Setup instructions
* Dependency requirements
* Testing commands
* Contribution guidelines

Skipping documentation creates unnecessary problems.

---

## Step 4: Install Dependencies

Most projects require dependencies.

Examples:

### Node.js

```bash id="npm-install"
npm install
```

### Bun

```bash id="bun-install"
bun install
```

### Python

```bash id="pip-install"
pip install -r requirements.txt
```

Always follow the project's instructions.

---

## Step 5: Run the Project

Before changing code:

Verify the project already works.

Example:

```bash id="run-project"
npm run dev
```

Or:

```bash id="start-project"
npm start
```

Expected workflow:

```text id="baseline"
Fresh Clone
↓
Runs Successfully
↓
Ready For Changes
```

This creates a known baseline.

---

## Step 6: Create a New Branch

Never work directly on the main branch.

Create a branch:

```bash id="new-branch"
git checkout -b fix-login-bug
```

Benefits:

* Easier reviews
* Cleaner history
* Safer experimentation

---

![Developer working on a feature branch inside a code editor](https://images.unsplash.com/photo-1461749280684-dccba630e2f6)

## Step 7: Reproduce the Problem

Before fixing anything:

```text id="bug-process"
Read Issue
↓
Reproduce Bug
↓
Understand Cause
```

If you can't reproduce the issue, fixing it becomes difficult.

---

## Step 8: Make Your Changes

Now modify the code.

Keep changes:

* Focused
* Small
* Relevant

Avoid unrelated modifications.

Maintainers appreciate clean contributions.

---

## Step 9: Run Existing Tests

Most projects include automated tests.

Examples:

```bash id="npm-test"
npm test
```

```bash id="vitest"
npm run test
```

```bash id="pytest"
pytest
```

Goal:

```text id="test-goal"
Existing Tests
↓
Pass Successfully
```

Your change should not break existing functionality.

---

## Step 10: Test the Feature Manually

Automated tests are helpful.

Manual testing is still important.

Verify:

* Expected behavior works
* UI looks correct
* No obvious regressions

Users experience the product, not the test suite.

---

## Step 11: Run Linters

Many repositories enforce code style.

Examples:

```bash id="eslint"
npm run lint
```

```bash id="fix-lint"
npm run lint:fix
```

Linters help catch:

* Formatting issues
* Syntax problems
* Code quality concerns

---

![Code quality checks and automated testing workflow](https://images.unsplash.com/photo-1489389944381-3471b5b30f04)

## Step 12: Review Your Changes

Before committing:

Ask:

* Does this solve the issue?
* Is unnecessary code included?
* Did I accidentally modify unrelated files?

A final review prevents surprises.

---

## Step 13: Commit Clearly

Good commit:

```text id="good-commit"
Fix login validation bug
```

Poor commit:

```text id="bad-commit"
update
```

Clear commit messages help reviewers understand changes quickly.

---

## Step 14: Push and Create a Pull Request

Push branch:

```bash id="push-branch"
git push origin fix-login-bug
```

Then open a pull request.

Include:

* Problem description
* Solution summary
* Testing details

This helps maintainers review efficiently.

---

## Common Local Testing Mistakes

### Skipping Setup Instructions

Always read documentation first.

---

### Not Running Existing Tests

Passing tests increase confidence.

---

### Making Huge Changes

Small pull requests are easier to review.

---

### Ignoring Lint Errors

Formatting issues create unnecessary review work.

---

### Testing Only Happy Paths

Try edge cases too.

---

## A Simple Testing Workflow

```text id="simple-workflow"
Fork Repository
↓
Clone Locally
↓
Install Dependencies
↓
Run Project
↓
Create Branch
↓
Make Changes
↓
Run Tests
↓
Manual Testing
↓
Submit PR
```

Following this process prevents many common issues.

---

## Benefits of Local Testing

Local testing helps:

* Catch bugs earlier
* Improve pull request quality
* Reduce CI failures
* Build contributor confidence
* Earn maintainer trust

The more reliable your contributions become, the easier future contributions will be.

---

## FAQ

### Do I need to run tests before every pull request?

Yes. It's one of the most important contributor responsibilities.

### What if the project has no tests?

Perform thorough manual testing and document what you tested.

### Should I create a new branch for every issue?

Yes. Separate branches keep contributions organized.

### What if I can't reproduce the bug?

Ask maintainers for clarification before attempting a fix.

### Are automated tests enough?

Usually not. Manual verification is still valuable.

---

## Final Thoughts

Testing locally is one of the simplest ways to improve your open source contributions.

It demonstrates professionalism, reduces maintainer workload, and helps ensure your changes actually solve the intended problem.

Before every pull request, remember:

```text id="final-flow"
Code
↓
Test
↓
Verify
↓
Submit
```

That small extra effort can dramatically increase the quality of your contributions and your success as an open source contributor.
